//: Differences from the pre-refactor baseline that are intended.
snapshot:verify compares against a capture taken before the module framework
existed. Anything not listed here is a regression. Anything listed here is a
decision someone made on purpose, with the reason next to it — which is the
whole point: the list of everything this refactor deliberately changed is one
reviewable file rather than a memory of which failures were 'fine'.
`path` is a JSON path into the captured file; everything under it is
accepted too, so '$.body.modules' covers the whole subtree. Use bracket
notation for a key containing dots: "$['report.csv']".

accepted.why: New key. Configured module instances. Empty on an installation whose settings.json predates modules — the registry derives the ActivoBank and Pricempire instances from the old `schedules` and `internal.profile` keys instead, so nothing that already existed changed value.

New endpoints, one group per configured instance: what the interface reads to know which modules exist and what each offers, each instance's configuration, and each one's status. The per-provider routes they generalise (/google/status, /pricempire/status, /ingest/activobank, …) all still exist and still answer exactly the same thing — the entries for those are compared as before, and are unchanged.

Not a captured file — recorded here so the one visible change in the interface is written down somewhere. The Settings schedules table now names each module from its manifest's translation key, so it reads 'Leitura do email ActivoBank' in Portuguese instead of the hardcoded English 'ActivoBank email scan'. The old list was a literal object of five English strings, which broke the rule that no user-visible text is a literal, and would have shown a fork's own bank as a bare id. Everything else on Connections, Rules and Settings is pixel-identical.

Gone from the capture, and they were noise. Documents are now re-read by the module instance that stored them; Pricempire declares no bank-document parser, so its portfolio exports are skipped. The baseline entries were those CSVs fed to the ActivoBank statement parsers, which read zero transactions out of a hundred rows each and reported one unparsed line — a measurement of nothing.

New endpoint. GET /api/analytics/flow, the income → account → category aggregate behind the Money flow card. Deliberately its own route rather than two more fields on /analytics: that response is in this baseline, and keeping it byte-identical is what makes this whole comparison a signal. Nothing asks for this endpoint unless a dashboard node is drawing it.
New endpoint. GET /api/analytics/daily, one row per day with spending, behind the Spending calendar card. Same reasoning as the flow route above.

New endpoint. GET /api/currency/rates, the whole exchange-rate table now that the app converts between forty-five currencies rather than two. The single-pair routes it generalises (/currency/rate and its refresh) are deliberately untouched and are compared as before — if either of those ever drifts, that is a bug in the wrapper, not a diff to accept.

Gone. It briefly held a flag per experimental chart. Those charts are now ordinary entries in the dashboard's widget catalogue, added and removed by the reader, so the flag was a second place to switch on something the add/remove gesture already governs.

New key. The cards the dashboard is made of, in the order they are drawn: {id, widget, view, size} per node. `view` lives on the node rather than in the browser, which is both how a view preference survives a restart and how the same widget can appear twice on one dashboard as a chart and as a table. The shipped default is six cards; this installation's own settings.json carries twelve, which is a data fact rather than a default.

New keys `rates` and `manual` beside the old `usdToEur`, which is still written and still holds the same number. Conversion used to be one dollar-to-euro scalar; it is now a table against the euro pivot, because the app ships fourteen languages and 'the dollar rate' is not a currency system. `loadSettings` migrates the scalar into `rates.USD` on read, so an installation that predates the table sees no change in what anything is worth.

Shape change: each entry is now {key, params} instead of a finished sentence. It was the last hardcoded Portuguese string the server put on screen — 'X% do que gastaste foi em Y' — which read Portuguese in all fourteen languages. Nothing in the interface renders this field today, so the visible effect is nil; the point is that it can now be rendered in the reader's language when something does.

//: Below this line: not caused by any code change. The baseline was captured
on 2026-08-11 and the ledger has lived since — quotes refreshed, a sync ran,
an appearance switch was flipped. They are listed rather than silently
tolerated so that the next person can tell a stale baseline from a
regression, which is the one distinction this file exists to preserve.
Re-taking the baseline would clear them and hide whatever drifted alongside.
accepted.why: api/assets.json, api/investments*.json, api/securities.json and api/analytics*.json allocation values move with the market — the CS2 position is 475.35 → 461.05 as of this writing, because the quote fetcher keeps running. api/events.json $.body.bytes grew with the ledger, which is 2912 movements in the baseline and 2989 now: statements have been ingested since, so api/transactions.json, api/accounts*.json, documents.json and everything derived from them differ by exactly that. api/settings.json $.body.appearance.locale went pt → en and $.body.appearance.textures false → true because the switches were flipped in Settings. Thirty-four of fifty-eight files differ on this count alone, and the same thirty-four differ with the dashboard work reverted — which is how it was checked. Re-taking the baseline would clear them and hide whatever drifted alongside.
